articles.text: Let’s elect proven local leaders Editor: In our small and very engaged community, we benefit most from leaders who are good listeners, who do their research, and who work well with others. As we’ve all experienced, so often the most difficult issues are ones that weren’t expected: for example, the impact of COVID on our schools, and the State-imposed requirement to plan for more housing in Piedmont. We need level-headed leaders who respond well to unexpected challenges by listening to all community members, who keep an open mind and seriously consider differing opinions, who study the options and consider all ramifications, and who work respectfully with staff and stakeholders in support of community goals. I wholeheartedly endorse Betsy Andersen and Jen Long for City Council. Betsy and Jen are both experienced attorneys who are also excellent listeners, clear thinkers, and thoughtful policy makers. As they have proven by their service on our City Council, Betsy and Jen ask good questions, meet with residents to navigate challenges, and look for creative opportunities to strengthen our community. articles.text: I subscribed to PREC’s newsletter when I was editor of the Piedmont Post because I understand the positive traction this group has in the community. PREC was formed during my tenure at the Post and I greatly value the good work this group does in the community. I’ve since left the Piedmont Post to pursue other journalistic endeavors. I’d like to add my unsolicited two cents, introduced with verbatim quotes from PREC’s newsletter dated September 22: “The PREC steering committee must correct the record: we did not create the website, nor do we have control over its content.” 1 – Please understand that letters to the editor are not factchecked by journalists and editors (especially if they do not name an elected official or office) in the same way a news story is. This is true in all publications, from Piedmont Post to the NY Times. Although NYT v Sullivan honed in on publishers’ liability with advertising, I would argue the same situation applies here. In this quote you are asking for leniency from those who read your published content, took it as fact, and still perceived it negatively; and yet, you ask a publication to review a published sample with to-the-line fact-checking. If the Post were to say, “we did not create the [letter to the editor], nor do we have control over its content,” would that be acceptable to you? My answer is no – of course you should review anything you publish. “We call upon the Post to follow up with a clarifying article and to stop publishing erroneous content” 2 – I believe that your call for the Post to “follow up with a clarifying article and to stop publishing erroneous contact” is self-serving at best. There is no clarification or expansion on what is considered “erroneous content” published – how does this help your readers? – there should be some supporting arguments since that is a fairly pointed statement. Think of letters to the editor as an open forum. In my opinion, the right thing to do would be to contact the publisher and ask for that person’s contact information to have an informed and educated dialogue. The decision you made was to attack the press – and, history will tell you better than I where that leads. “If the Post had contacted us, PREC would have been happy to clarify” 3 – I have worked with Piedmont Post since PREC’s inception. Only a handful of times did anyone at PREC send me a press release. I received this newsletter after my departure and was stunned. The newsletter is authored by seven individuals and should offer a contact for reporters to follow-up. In this case, someone who did not author the article is assumed to have written the article, which would be used as a quote. I had a great rapport with many organizations in Piedmont, but PREC never reached out to me or the Post for publicity, whereas the others took initiative. My point being – help us help you but fostering a relationship with press. The Post, Mercury, EBX, many would love to hear and publish what you’re doing. As a layperson and not press, I strongly ask you to hear all dialogue as you approach issues that the community holds at heart. I promise you it won’t all be nice, as is the nature of community dialogue. This newsletter felt pointed and angry, both at a local publication and a resident. This made me sad as a journalist knowing the relationship I had with PREC was minimal. I felt as though I should have done more to promote and highlight the good work you do, and yet, slamming a local publication seems antithetical to your mission of transparency. Quite literally, journalism is the only profession protected by the constitution. We take our jobs seriously – which is why now, even after leaving, I was personally offended by this newsletter. I truly hope all has been amended and that a fluid relationship between PREC and the Post can be fostered. I understand that a very productive meeting took place in the Post’s office last Friday at the invitation of the Post. I believe we are all hoping it Will benefit all community leaders, members, and stakeholders in the long run.
articles.title: In response to recent assertions by PREC

articles.text: Editor: In its September 21, 2022, issue, the Piedmont Post published a letter from Tu Ngoc Nguyen asserting that the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC) created a website, PiedmontVotes.com, that “smears” several candidates in the upcoming election. The PREC steering committee must correct the record: We did not create the PiedmontVotes.com website, nor do we have control over its content. We shared the site’s link in our newsletter because it was the only resource we found that had collected public information about all candidates. If anyone is upset by the site’s content, please note that: 1) The website is a compilation of candidates’ public statements and other publicly available information. 2) Concerns should be sent through the website itself to the site’s creator. In addition, counter to the claim in Nguyen’s letter that PREC is anti-Asian, we point out that the PREC steering committee supports an Asian American candidate, three of our steering committee members are Asian American, and we organized the only anti-Asian hate solidarity event in our city to speak out against Asian hate. Facts do matter. Let’s keep the focus of the upcoming elections on the most important issues that will help our schools and city move forward in creating a great community for all. –The PREC Steering Committee: Amy Whalen Griffith Deb Leland Diana Lee Fairuz Abdullah Irene Cheng Sarah Karlinsky Susy Struble prec-steering@googlegroups.com

I was unable to find any candidate endorsements by PREC on their website, but I did go to the piedmontvotes.com site to review the smear campaign against Shirley Hooi that had so upset the writer. I cannot see how posting public letters from Ms. Hooi to the Piedmont Post and a public statement about an Exedra article, without comment one way or the other, can be characterized as a “smear campaign”. What I read on the Piedmont Votes site are Ms. Hooi’s own words accompanied by a single letter from another citizen correcting Ms. Hooi’s representation of critical race theory and challenging the notion that it is being taught, or contemplating being taught, to young children in our public schools. This is a “smear”? Further, to imply through rhetorical questions that PREC and what was posted on the Piedmont Votes site contributes to the climate of Asian hate – indeed “encourages attacks” – is, well, beyond any objective reading of the contents, to put it as politely as I can. In my view, such baseless accusations diminish the tragic reality of the actual threats and attacks faced by persons of Asian descent in our society today, and the shameful history of discrimination, threats, and attacks visited upon Asians in America (about which I learned nothing when I was in public school). I read Ms. Hooi’s letters to the editor when they were first published. I thought it unfortunate to see the contentious – and, in my opinion, false – narratives promoted in those letters enter into the public discourse in our small town. The writer is “embarrassed” and laments that there is “divisive national politicking” in Piedmont. I sympathize and agree; and that is why I won’t be voting for Shirley Hooi. –Bill Brizendine Anonymous websites do not serve our kids Editor: As a candidate for school board in November, I’m responding to a letter in last week’s Piedmont Post that pointed to an anonymous website sharing the past letters and editorials of candidates like myself. The website draws from publicly available information online; however, it fails to name the owner or group behind the site. I want to state clearly that I am unequivocally opposed to any website that hides behind anonymity, while degrading civil discourse in our community. It’s extremely disheartening to see anonymous outreach and communication become a staple of political discussion in our town. Last year, we saw an anonymous online survey posted by a group called Piedmonters for Fair Education, which asked the school community to report on Piedmont teachers who discussed diversity in a way that offended the group’s politics. This tactic is reprehensible. It is reminiscent of authoritarian governments that break down the bonds between citizens by asking neighbors to spy on each other. I call on my fellow candidates running for office to condemn the use of anonymous political websites that attempt to stifle candid discussion or intimidate community members. I also want to correct an error in last week’s letter stating that there is a “lone Asian running for school board.” I am the daughter of immigrants from India, who came to the United States with extremely limited resources to attend school and improve the opportunities available to them. Knowing the tenacity and resilience needed to pursue that dream, and knowing what they have overcome to build a life in the Bay Area, I am extremely proud of who they are and what they have accomplished. Like many children of immigrants, I have deep appreciation for my heritage and strive to instill the same sense of pride in my children. I would like to stress that I am my own candidate. While I value endorsements and support from individuals and groups that are aligned with me in the priorities I see for the school district, one of my campaign promises is to increase dialogue and transparency among community members so that all stakeholder voices are heard. I encourage voters to attend the League of Women Voters’ Candidate Forum on Thursday Sept. 29 at 7 pm, where you will have a chance to hear directly from all three candidates and learn about our platforms and priorities. Our children deserve more than voting for the loudest person in the room shouting half-truths. articles.text: from the City of Piedmont The City of Piedmont is currently updating the Housing Element of the City’s General Plan , which outlines the policies and programs that will guide g rowth and development in within Piedmont over the next 8 yea rs. Community involvement is essential to shaping this docu ment. To that end, the City of Piedmont is sharing t hese facts about the Housing Element that every resident should know. Lea rn more about the Housing Element update process at P P i i e e d d m m o o n n t t i i s s H H o o m m e e . .o o r r g g . FACT: Adopting an updated Housing Element IS NOT OPTIONAL. The State of California requires all cities to update their Housing Element every 8 years to accommodate their assigned Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA). The updated Housing Element must receive certification from the FACT: Putting the draft Housing Element to the voters as a ballot initiative would diminish—not enhance—local control. Voting on the Housing Element would not eliminate any requirement for Piedmont to comply with State law. Failure to adopt an updated Housing Element by the State mandated deadline could result in harsh and costly fines and could limit Piedmont’s authority over future local land use decisions. FACT: The City Charter does not require a vote on the type of zoning changes proposed in the draft Housing Element. Piedmont’s City Charter (Sec 9.01) gives the City Council authority over the General Plan, which includes the Housing Element. Adding uses or changing densities to existing zones does not require voter approval. FACT: The Housing Element does not require Piedmont to build 587 units of new housing. The Housing Element only plans for the CAPACITY for development of new housing. It does not require the actual development or construction of those housing units. FACT: The City government itself would not build housing. Any development being planned in the Housing Element would be carried out by individual property owners and private developers. FACT: Affordable housing is less than half of the City’s allocation. Piedmont’s allocation includes 257 affordable (low and very low income) units, 92 moderate income units, and 238 above moderate income units, for a total of 587. FACT: The City cannot reduce its RHNA allocation or otherwise get out of updating its Housing Element. Piedmont submitted seven letters to the Association of Bay Area Governments (ABAG) articulating concerns about the 6th cycle housing allocations. Due in part to these actions, our mandate is 50% less than many comparable cities. The period for appeals is over. If the City had appealed to ABAG, we would have risked increasing our numbers. All appeals to ABAG were rejected except for one that involved an incorrect jurisdictional boundary. FACT: The Draft Housing Element DOES NOT include “high-density” apartment buildings throughout Piedmont. The current draft does not propose allowing apartment buildings in single-family areas, which comprise about 86% of land in Piedmont. The draft proposes increasing allowed density only in existing commercial/mixed use areas, public facilities, and multifamily zones, as well as for houses of worship building on their own property. Visit PiedmontIsHome.org to learn more, share comments, and stay informed about Piedmont’s Housing Element update. Questions? Contact us at piedmontishome@piedmont.ca.gov.

This year’s campaign chairs are Dana Murray, Julia Ruthven and Katie Sharafi, supported by the Piedmont Education Foundation staff and a dedicated group of volunteers. Over a marathon few months this team will put up banners at the schools, conduct community outreach, write personal letters, and make hundreds of phone calls. “We start planning the next Giving Campaign as soon as the current one ends,” said PEF executive director Heather Frank, “The messaging, outreach, events, and materials represent months of work from the office team and dozens of volunteers.” A nearly unprecedented California budget surplus has provided a one-time infusion of additional funds for the coming school year, allowing the Giving Campaign to reduce the requested per-child donation from prior years. This year, the team asks that families donate $1,980 representing the funding gap for each student. “Even when the state has a surplus, there’s still an enormous funding gap that needs to be filled by the community,” says Sharafi. The requested amount will help cover the difference between what the district receives from other funding sources and the cost of providing the quality of education that students receive in Piedmont. “We are asking for less per student but working to have increased participation rates this year,” said Sharafi. “We want everyone to participate and hope families will give a gift that is Wildwood students Isabelle Wheeler (left), Margot Miller, James DiPiazza, Nina Meyer, Liana Shahid, and Piper Lang. meaningful to them.” Last year’s record-breaking Giving Campaign raised $3.7 million for Piedmont schools. “Parents and community members dug deep, but overall participation was still down from preCOVID levels,” said Frank, “We want everyone to understand that participation matters. A donation of any amount makes a real difference for our schools.” The funds from the Giving Campaign will help keep Piedmont class sizes small and fund a broad array of student needs, from wellness to classroom aides to libraries and the arts. “I’ve always seen our family contribution to the Giving Campaign as an investment, not a gift,” says Sharafi. “You really do see the return on that investment in the caliber of the teachers and staff.” To learn more about the Piedmont Education Foundation’s Giving Campaign or to make a donation, visit www.piedmontedfoundation.org. Aside from exciting new technology, there are also special items like 245 Silver Snoopy pins, a Moon rock from Apollo 11 and a USB with essays from the Artemis essay contest. One of the essays launching with Artemis 1 was written and submitted by teen Galaxy Explorer, Sowmya. In her essay, titled Yin for the Win, the high school student considers what it would be like to lead a lunar expedition, including who she would bring and what she would leave behind. She imagines an all-woman crew exploring and collecting samples on the South Pole. Two years after submitting her essay, she is finally watching her ideas launch with Artemis 1. “I feel honored that the words I wrote are on a USB on Artemis I,” said Sowmya, “To think, something I wrote is aboard the most powerful rocket ever made and will go to the Moon and back!” Fifty years after the Apollo missions, NASA is preparing to send the first woman and person of color to the Moon by 2025. While Sowmya has read about and learned about past space missions, the Artemis program will be the first time she will witness astronauts stepping foot on the lunar surface. “It’s electrifying to think of the discoveries Artemis will make and the possibilities it and seismometers to discover lunar properties. articles.text: Part 3 in a series In advance of the November 8 Municipal Election, six candidates have filed papers for three available seats on the Piedmont City Council. They were asked to answer the following two questions, which were sent to them on Thursday, September 22. This marks week 3 of the Post’s election coverage. Next week the focus will return to the school board candidates. Beginning with the October 12 edition, the Post’s weekly coverage will include questions and answers from both City Council and School Board candidates until the election on November 8. Week 3 QUESTIONS 1. What do you consider as the City’s most pressing problems? How do you plan to address them? 2. If elected, how do you plan to make yourself available to residents? ment. As a current Councilmember, my contact information is available on the City’s website. My email and phone number are also published in the Piedmont Post each week. If residents have any questions for me about the election, please reach out to me via my campaign website Betsyforpiedmont.us. and decide on options by a vote is not only necessary but legally required. directly tied to my strong desire to engage the community beyond the limited confines of City Council meetings. 2. Availability This year I transitioned from partner to “of counsel” at my law firm which allows me to devote more time to civic and non-profit service. My years of legal and tax experience has prepared me to better serve the city of Piedmont. For decades I have reviewed and responded to daily emails and calls with clients who expect a prompt response. I will extend that same diligence and respect to the residents of Piedmont. Resident communication is of paramount importance to finding solutions. To that end, I intend to dialogue with individuals in the community through email, phone, social media channels, and with monthly “office hours” in a hybrid setting. Finally, I expect to use door knocking when necessary to educate residents and solicit their participation on important issues. There should be no surprises. NANCY BOSTROM 1. Most pressing problem Safety is the #1 issue. People say they live here for the schools, but it’s really the safety. When there is safety the mosques, synagogues and churches, scouts, schools, libraries, choirs, can do their jobs. I ran before and wanted cameras at every Piedmont entrance. I didn’t win, but you did. After the election, cameras were installed. I suggest using armored cars for our Police. I suggest we arm our teachers and provide 160 hours of training like the police. 2. Availability I am going to be handing out plans and ideas for ADU’s which I think are the answer to a lot of our concerns. You can find me at most Piedmont functions, and at the coffee hour at Piedmont Community Church. You can phone me at 203 998-1776 and email me at winstonmalloryboston@gmail.com. BETSY ANDERSEN Incumbent 1. Most pressing problem In the short term, the most pressing issue is to complete the 6th cycle state-mandated Housing Element plan. Every California city is required to have a state-certified Housing Element plan that is updated every eight years. As a City Councilmember, I think the most important thing I can do is to be transparent about this process, listen to all ideas and concerns, and make information available. Please visit the City of Piedmont housing website Piedmontishome.org where you can find answers to FAQs, legal analyses, links to meetings and informational videos, and much more. Over the next four years, we need to focus on our aging civic buildings. Our Police and Fire Departments operate out of spaces that are between 70 to 110 years old. We are currently in the process of renovating the 911 Dispatch Center. If re-elected, I will continue to support efforts to bring our city buildings up to current standards. 2. Availability I welcome all opportunities to talk and meet with residents. I love participating in community events, and I am always happy to attend meetings with local civic and school organizations. While Councilmembers are unpaid volunteers and do not have office space at City Hall, I am happy to schedule meetings in the City Hall conference room or (weather permitting) outside in one of our beautiful parks. Piedmont is a great place to live because our residents are engaged – volunteering their time and talents – at every level of our local governBRIDGET HARRIS 1. Most pressing problem At this time I believe the City’s most pressing problem is the divisiveness of the Housing Element. I believe the discord originates from both the communication and the process. There is no need for rancor; we need to join together for a solution. Having been made aware of the Housing Element late in the development, I understand the need for more effective disclosure and inclusion by the residents of Piedmont. Increasing the population by approximately 10% and housing units by 15% is a substantial change for our small city. Broad public participation and true engagement by an election process will help unify the city and increase the likelihood of a fair and successful outcome. Delaying submission of a Housing Element Plan until all of Piedmont has the chance to understand the consequences JENNIFER LONG Incumbent 1. Most pressing problem Our most pressing issue is hiring a strong leader to fill the vacancy that will be left when our current City Administrator, Sara Lillevand, retires in April 2023. This crucial leadership role oversees essential city services including fire and police; infrastructure and planning; and parks and recreation. The City Administrator also provides oversight of budget development and spending. As our city works to comply with a state housing mandate, the City Administrator serves as an ambassador and advocate for Piedmont’s interests. We need to make sure Piedmont hires someone who invites constituent input, listens and learns, and puts forth solid recommendations for the Council to act upon. As a City Council member, I will work to ensure that we hire a strong leader who will successfully advance important projects like the new pool construction and the state-mandated housing plan. 2. Availability Connecting with Piedmont residents is one of my favorite things to do as a City Council member. As a current member of Council I am regularly invited to meet with organizations and individuals. Community events such as the recent “Cops, Coffee, and Cars” are opportunities for me to speak to residents, deepen my understanding of community perspectives, and hear new ideas. When elected, I am looking to be even more accessible by creating “office hours,” which will be a scheduled day and time when I am available to talk with community members. My reason for expanding my availability is JEANNE SOLNORDAL 1. Most pressing problem Housing Element – Cycle 6, is the most pressing problem facing our community. Finding space for 587 units is extremely challenging. Unfortunately, the city did not appeal the allocation, therefore we have lost our right to join any future lawsuits that may be filed against the state. The city agreed to the 587 units without protest. This was fiscally irresponsible, as taxpaying residents will bear the cost of the civic services needed by the new residents. So where do we put them? City center, Moraga Canyon/ Blair Park are unfeasible as traffic, parking and children/ pedestrian safety are an issue. Accessory dwelling units will offset our requirement, but their numbers are minimal and will not eliminate the need for a large build. The only sites I see we could consider are multi-story units on Grand Avenue or at Zion Lutheran Church. Both sites would require owner participation and a rezoning vote. 2. Availability I am already available to residents. As president of a local organization, I am always reaching out. As a city council member representing the community, it is important to always keep an open-door policy. My home is always open, and my email and phone number are in many directories. I am always available for a conversation, regardless of subject, now and in the future. Some of the softest voices in Piedmont are our seniors. I will make a concerted effort to get to know every senior personally. I will check in on them on a regular basis to ensure their needs and concerns are being addressed. I will advocate for senior services just as we advocate for our youth. Please reach out at votesolnordal@gmail.com or 510-368-8880. TOM RAMSEY 1. Most pressing problem For several budget cycles, our City Administrator, our Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee and City staff have listed critical infrastructure as Piedmont’s most pressing problem. I agree. It’s past time to make needed upgrades to Piedmont’s aging infrastructure and facilities. Our critical facilities need to be made safe, so our first responders can keep us safe. I also agree that our financial stewardship includes an obligation to plan for the substantial repair / replacement of our facilities. The facility upgrade process will take time, robust public engagement, careful consideration of the phasing of work, and a commitment to seamlessly deliver excellent public services during the work. I’ve spent 30 years working as an architect tackling this type of work for commercial clients. I’ll put that experience to work for Piedmont. 2. Availability The best part of this campaign has been getting to meet new people and reconnecting with neighbors. If elected, I’ll expand connecting with residents by: • Encouraging participation because public engagement improves our decision-making process. Our town is home to an impressive depth of expertise. This collective wealth of experience is a great resource and I’ll leverage that resource as much as possible. • Transparent communication. I believe that transparency is a best practice to promote accountability. I’ll always make myself available via email, a chat at a public event or better yet, a conversation over coffee at Mulberry’s. And as I’ve done for the past 7 years through my service on the Planning Commission, I’ll listen first, ask questions, read every letter, and work together to make decisions with Piedmont’s best interest front and center.

articles.text: In a strong week for Piedmont’s tennis team, the Highlanders defeated North Coast Section rival Lick Wilmerding 4-3 in San Francisco on Tuesday, September 20, and followed up two days later with a mighty 6-1 victory at Castro Valley on Thursday. The victory over Lick came against a Div. 2 North Coast Section opponent, which will help Piedmont earn a higher seeding in the NCS tournament at the end of the season.. “This was a very satisfying win over Lick Wilmerding,” said coach Jim Landes. “It shows we are in a good position to compete well in the NCS championships at the end of the season. But we must keep working to improve,” After the 6-1 win over Castro Valley Piedmont remained undefeated against WACC opponents, They earlier had beaten Bishop O’Dowd in a tournament in Fresno, and San Leandro and Arroyo in league matches. The tournament victory over O’Dowd means Piedmont has technically played just three league matches. The Highlanders are challenging to be the top team in its league, with Berkeley and Alameda likely being the other two contenders. 4-3 win over Lick Wilmerding Piedmont won all of its matches in straight sets against Lick, splitting the four singles matches and winning two of three doubles matches. At singles, No. 1 starter Tanya Kononova made quick work of her opponent in an easy 6-1, 6-1 victory. At No. 2, Anne Jumper lost 6-1, 6-1. Carolina Romanczuk at No. 3 won in straight sets 6-3, 6-1, and at No. 4, Annika Gilliland lost 6-1, 6-2. “Tanya trounced her opponent while Anne probably played their real No. 1 starter. articles.text: Piedmont’s cross country teams ran away with victories at the first league meet of the season at Hayward High on Wednesday, September 21. The boys’ team won with 39 points, and the girls won with 58 points, PHS junior Xander Schulte-Sasse led his team by placing 2nd in a field of 84 runners, and freshman Skylar Best led the girls’ team with a 2nd place overall finish out of 59 runners. “Everyone is coming to practice, working hard with real effort, and it is paying off,” said Piedmont coach Jeanine Holmlund. “Consistency matters. Piedmont scored against six Shoreline teams in our first WACC League meet, so our record now stands at 6-0,” It marked the second appearance for the cross country team and first official look at the complete team for both the boys and girls. Boys results Schulte-Sasse led the way for the boys with a time of 15:27.57 on the three-mile course. His time was a personal record by 36 seconds. He’s begun to install himself as the squad’s top runner after placing 21st of 222 at the Lowell Invitational, and clocking 15:33 at a scrimmage meet on August 27. Behind Schulte-Sasse was senior Parker Long finishing fourth with a time of 15:52.1, also a personal record by 24 seconds. In seventh was senior Christian Taylor, crossing the line in 16:10.89, while junior Julien Lee was right behind in eighth with a time of 16:16.81. Rounding out the top five times was sophomore and first-year varsity runner Evan Byun in 18th, clocking a 17:05.26. Girls results Best led the girls with a time of 19:32.24, claiming 2nd overall. She’s been an eye-catching freshman on the team by placing 12th of 204 runners at the Lowell Invitational Frosh/Soph event earlier this month, and fourth out of 74 runners at a scrimmage meet on August 27 at Hayward’s threemile course. Right behind Best was junior Jamie Schwarz in third with a time of 20:30.93, and junior Josie Oesterer in fifth in 19:51.50. Next in for PHS was freshman Cora Chun in 19th, clocking a 20:56.30, while another freshman, Elia Kwong, rounded out the top five placing 31st in 21:52.34. NEXT UP Piedmont looks ahead to hosting the Be The G.O.A.T. (Greatest Of All Time) Invitational at the Pinole Multi-Use Trails outside Hercules on Saturday, October 1 at 9:00 a.m. It marks the second time PHS will host the event. Xander Schulte-Sasse was Piedmont’s top runner in second with a time of 15:27.57, which marked a personal record for the junior athlete. Christian Taylor placed seventh with a time of 16:10.89.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s football team, hanging on by a thread, suffered its fourth straight loss on Friday, September 23 at Witter Field, falling to St. Mary’s 49-15. With a depleted roster and additional players now out with injuries, it was an uphill fight for survival. The game saw former Piedmont head coach John Trotman’s return to Witter Field, now as head coach at St. Mary’s. His team has a 4-0 record. The Panthers ended the first quarter leading 14-0 and went into halftime up 35-0. Piedmont scored one touchdown in the third quarter and closed the game with a touchdown and a two-point conversion in the final minute. “We had a lot of opportunities; it was more of us just defeating ourselves. Although Piedmont took a beating with a sophomore-laden varsity roster, the second half showed some bright spots. The Highlanders’ execution noticeably improved, including the recovery of an onside kick at the start of the second half. “It was encouraging that we didn’t just pack it in and call it a night [when we were] down 35-0. It’s hard to come back after that. I wanted to get the momentum going and catch them sleeping with a quick kick. We just wanted to create some momentum and walk out with our head high feeling good about something,” said Seiden. articles.text: Final performance is Sunday, October 2 Shotgun Players’ Man of God, written by playwright Anna Ouyang and directed by Michelle Talgarow, ends this Sunday, October 2. Tickets are available online for shows on Thursday through Sunday, September 29-October 2. Man of God is inspired by a real-life incident at a Christian mission in Southeast Asia. The comedy, described by the playwright as a “feminist thriller,” follows four students Mimi (Lauren Andrei Garcia), Samantha (Alexandra Lee), (Joyce Domanico-Huh), and KyungHwa (Sharon Shao) while on a church mission to Bangkok. The girls, visiting from Southern California, discover a hidden camera in their hotel room that they conclude was placed by the church pastor. “I wrote the play in part to examine my own desire for and participation in the concept of the ‘revenge fantasy’ narrative that our culture is so fond of and the way that narrative can fail survivors of sexual abuse who are unable to enact those fantasies in reality,” said Ouyang. Man of God runs 90 minutes without an intermission at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. The play will be available to stream online beginning October 5. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse celebrates its 20th season with the debut of Indecent on September 22. The show will run through November 5. Paula Vogel’s play is based on the real-life events of Sholem Asch’s The God of Vengeance. Although many consider Asch’s work to be a seminal work of Jewish culture, it is also viewed by some as traitorous libel. “We were lucky enough to be on hand when Paula Vogel’s Indecent opened on Broadway five years ago. Being huge fans of hers already, and galvanized by the production, we began angling to present the play’s Bay Area premiere,” said San Francisco Playhouse Artistic Director Bill English. “At the time we were a long shot due to strong interest from bigger companies, but after a two-year pandemic and catastrophic changes in American theatre, a door opened five years later for us to present it.” The play is directed by Susi Damilano, with music direction by Dmitri Gaskin and choreography by Nicole Helfer. The principal cast members include Dean Linnard, Billy Cohen, Rachel Botchan, and Rivka Borek. The production is co-produced with the Yiddish Theatre Ensemble and features klezmer music. “It is both a love song to the Ashkenazi Jewish culture spanning 50 years, and a love song to the theatre. It is an odyssey that spins us from Warsaw to Berlin, to NY Yiddish theatre, to Broadway and back to Warsaw as the tumultuous and tragic history of the early 20th Century unfolds around the play within our play,” English explained. Jonathan Spector’s play weaves together the story of Stalin’s daughter who defected to America through protagonist Natalya (Anna Ishida) as she works through a horrible calamity. Natalya is considering divorce and a move to her homeland Russia. She believes her grandmother’s connections to Stalin might help, and the story begins a deep-dive into her family history as her husband Lukesh (Rajesh Bose) tries to persuade her to return. The play is directed by Aurora Artistic Director Josh Costello. Aurora Theatre Company is located at 2081 Addison Street in Berkeley. articles.text: Last Wednesday, a scant few hours after the Post reported on protests by unpaid ushers, Berkeley Rep abruptly reversed direction and cancelled its policy requiring the ushers to show up an extra half hour earlier for performances. The Front of House (FOH) Director, who instituted the policy that caused the protests, liberalized the prior policy by allowing ushers to arrive 15 minutes later than in the past. An email from Berkeley Rep dated 11:32 a.m. on September 21 stated: “We are going to shut down the combined FOH/BO ‘Team’ experience. It seems that ushers in general do not want to so [sic] this. I will start working on a seperate [sic] usher group that will work events, giftshop etc. with the FOH Team. Ushers in this group can come 15-30 minutes befor [sic] the lobby opens. Sign in - get you [sic] badge and go to your assigned door. This goes into effect today.” While the timing of the email might seem a bit coincidental, it’s reasonable to assume that someone higher up at Berkeley Rep was notified about the article and decided it was time to de-escalate the situation. The email must have resulted in a number of questions, because a few hours later, the FOH Director sent out a second, all bold email to cut off the discussion: “Hello Ushers, please just focus on ushering. Let us get through Goddess and Ripple. The other program is not happening yet. I have to build it [sic] I have no other information for you at this time. As soon as I get a clearer picture of what the ‘event ushers’ will be, I will reach out. This will be next season if it is approved.” While this appears to have put the matter to rest for the remainder of the current season, the status quo has not been totally restored. At least one usher who questioned the new policy and asked to be removed until the old policy was restored has not yet been reinstated. That person has emailed the FOH Director multiple times since Wednesday and has left a voicemail, all without a response. The Post will continue to follow the situation as it unfolds. Wily Hoag is the Piedmont Post’s Consumer Affairs Reporter.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep backtracks after Piedmont Post report

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum in San Francisco is currently exhibiting Filipino artist Carlos Villa’s work. His work will be on view through October 24. San Francisco-born Villa was a groundbreaking, 20th century modern artist whose work explores the meaning of cultural diversity in America. The exhibition, entitled Carlos Villa: Worlds in Collision, focuses mainly on the artist’s drawings, mixed-media painting, and constructions from the 1970s up until his death in 2013. Villa experimented with techniques of Western painting with materials found in non-Western art; the juxtaposition is most notably in the 1970s. The exhibition is a joint effort by the Asian Art Museum and San Francisco Art Institute (SFAI). Visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org/exhibitions/carlos-villa-worlds-in-collision/ to learn more.

articles.text: Charlie Callas and Sean Marshall (as the voice of Elliot the Dragon) in Pete’s Dragon. Review by Chris Honoré Pete’s Dragon is a movie aimed squarely at the 10-year-old demographic and never wavers, avoiding inside jokes or frenetic, over-the-top chase scenes that might appeal to the accompanying adults. Here’s the wonderful assumption that the filmmakers build on: kids believe in magic. They don’t have to push very hard to get the pre-tween crowd to suspend their disbelief and buy into a sweet premise involving a young boy (not exactly a feral child but not far from Mowgli, either). His only friend, Elliot, happens to be a 24-foot tall, furry green dragon. Yep. And when he sneezes you have to reach for a towel. But first things first: A young boy, Pete (Oakes Fegley), only five, is on a vacation adventure with his mom and dad in the Pacific Northwest. He’s in the backseat of their station wagon, reading an illustrated story titled, Elliot Gets Lost. Suddenly his father swerves to miss a deer and rolls the car. Pete is thrown clear, uninjured. His parents are killed. Panicked, alone, surrounded by strange sounds, he runs into the forest where he is surrounded by wolves. Unexpectedly, he is saved by Elliot, the dragon, who takes the boy under his wing, so-tospeak, and nurtures and cares for him (seeming half parent and half pet), helping him build an elaborate tree house. Six years pass. Pete seems to have thrived, and he and Elliot have now formed a deep and abiding bond. One day, a group of loggers, who have penetrated deep into the forest, appear and Pete is captivated by these men in their trucks and large bulldozers, signaling the encroachment of a civilization of which he is complete unaware. And now begins the juxtaposition of two realities – Pete’s natural world, and a world that is filled with cars and hospitals and people, such as forest ranger Grace (Bryce Dallas Howard) who watches over Pete as he struggles to cope. For decades, in this small northern logging town, called Millhaven, there has existed the legend of a dragon that lived deep in the woods, sighted rarely. No matter the witness, such sightings have always been immediately discounted as fantasy or perhaps simply wind in the high trees. One such purveyor of the Millhaven dragon legend is a wizened woodcarver (Robert Redford), who, like Pete, believes that if we look hard enough magic will reveal itself to us. His daughter, Grace, is a lifelong skeptic. What happens next will be embraced by the youngsters without question, as is the relationship between Elliot and Pete. There’s magic in this world if we are only open to letting it into our lives, amazing things are possible. Magic can transform our lives. The way it has transformed Pete’s. What is wonderful about this film is that Pete also discovers that there is magic in being enfolded in the collective arms of a family and that the two are not mutually exclusive. Kids love this stuff. Pete’s Dragon. Directed by Don Chaffey. Voiced by Helen Reddy, Mickey Rooney, Red Buttons. 2 hrs., 14 min. Rated PG. Released in 1977 as a fusion of animation and reallife. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: swaps his aloha shirt for western Just when you thought computer-generated imagery (CGI) had peaked, the folks at Industrial Light and Magic (ILM), under the direction of Gore Verbinksi (Pirates of the Caribbean), create Rango, an animated feature film that is a showstopper. It’s a marvel, done brilliantly in 2D, no less, with attention to detail that is unlike anything created thus far. The essential story is classic, a familiar Western trope. It begins with a thespian lizard in his terrarium (a small pool, a palm tree, and a plastic fish), riding in the back of a car. The family is driving across the Mojave Desert when they hit a bump in the road and the terrarium and lizard are bounced out, landing in the road, while the car continues out of sight. And so the lizard – a chameleon of sorts, blue-skinned, bugeyed, wearing an aloha shirt – stands on the side of the road as the sizzling sun leaches moisture out of everything. Parched, he makes his way across the desert to a town called Dirt, inhabited by an array of critters – rodents, lizards, Gila monsters – all desperate for water. Dirt, according to the mayor (Ned Beatty), is having a small drought. The remaining water, so precious, is in a bank vault. Our aloha lizard walks into a saloon where, when challenged, creates a persona and a story that is so authentic that he is quickly viewed as a savior and as the next sheriff. The stranger calls himself Rango (Johnny Depp) and soon duds. Unbeknownst to the townsfolk, Rango is a tenderfoot, a true dude, about to go up against the meanest, gnarliest, most conniving set of desert critters imaginable, all in on something nefarious. And all the dude is packing is his faux story (he killed a mess of outlaws with one shot, he says) and a rusty six-gun with only one bullet in the chamber. Wearing his tin star, his spurs jingling, Rango has to ride hard, shoot straight, and eventually face down hombres like Bad Bill (Ray Winstone) and Rattlesnake Jake (Bill Nighy), all while trying not to flinch. His life is further complicated when he meets Beans (Isla Fisher), a sweet little thing, also a lizard, who is fighting with the shifty, underhanded, no’count Mayor (Ned Beatty) over selling her pappy’s ranch. Close your eyes and you can hear a spaghetti-western soundtrack. Keep the faith, buckaroos, and you will meet the Spirit of the West, a leathery, tough-as-nails cowboy ridin’ his golf cart across some pretty mean territory, a lean question mark of a man who gives Rango some darned good advice. Are ya feeling lucky? Well, are ya? This is a great movie. But the writing is so adult, the jokes and vocabulary at times so dang highfalutin, that a lot of what is said will sail right over the heads of the peanut gallery. But no worries. There’s enough adventure packed into Rango for both audiences. Which is a good thing. Rango. Directed by Gore Verbinski. Animated. Voiced by Johnny Depp, Bill Nighy, Alfred Molina. 1 hr., 45 min. articles.text: Part 53 I was so impressed to read of the Safer and Cleaner School Commute event (Walk and Roll) in last week’s Piedmont Post. Maybe you read it. Piedmont High senior Skye Yeh, as part of her Girl Scout Gold Award program, came up with a plan to mitigate the crowded “unsafe” dropoff and pick-up situation in front of Wildwood School. Simple as can be, the event, with the cooperation of the school and police authorities, encouraged students to walk, scooter or bike to school from home. With 78% of students participating, the one-day event was nothing but a complete success! What a simple solution to a growing national trend/problem. I had a chance to talk with Skye recently, and as part of her program she astutely listed the benefits of getting to school without a car. Healthy exercise is high on the list: not only does it benefit the body, but as she put it, in the morning “it gets your brain going too.” That is a fact backed up by numerous scientific studies, such as Dr. John Ratey at Harvard Medical School who writes that morning exercise substantially improves learning in schools. The other obvious benefit is the pollution reduction of fewer cars on the road. Even with electric cars and their highly reduced carbon footprint, there is still environmental impact from the energy production to charge batteries, the manufacturing processes, and the end of useful life treatment of recycling. Safety and congestion is another issue. Sitting in a line of cars waiting is at best frustrating for everyone; the more cars on the road, especially in a small drop-off area, the less safe is the auto-pedestrian mix, especially with children involved. Sketches by Will Adams Skye also suggests that walking, scootering and biking is both friendly and fun, not only with classmates but with the community through which students pass on their way to school. While automobile travel is a part of the human DNA in our era, there are clearly downsides. Solutions to the inherent problems involve mitigating the exclusivity of car transportation – providing alternative ways of getting places. Certainly not everyone can walk or bike everywhere, but as Skye Yeh has recently shown us, most of us can walk at least some of the time to some places. Even eliminating a small proportion of auto trips reduces congestion, pollution, the need for so many parking spaces, and at the same time can enhance, rather than compromise our destinations. If you have a family member who has been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, or is starting to show symptoms, you will face some real challenges. Navigating the Alzheimer’s experience involves a long journey, and there’s no easy answer for how you can cope with your emotions. But you can at least address some of the financial issues involved to help give yourself a greater sense of control. Here are some moves to consider: • Plan for care costs and identify insurance coverage. The list of Alzheimer’s-related medical expenses is long and includes ongoing medical treatment, medical equipment, home safety modifications, prescription drugs and personal care supplies. As a caregiver, you’ll want to know the extent of your loved one’s health insurance: Medicare, supplemental policies, veteran’s benefits if applicable, and so on. One big question is how much coverage they might have for adult day care services, in-home care services and full-time residential care services, and other long-term care options. Long-term care is one of the largest health care costs not covered by Medicare, so you’ll want to determine if your loved one has a long-term care policy or another insurance policy with a long-term care rider. • Identify assets and debts. You’ll need to know your family member’s financial position, both what they own – bank accounts, investments, property, etc. – and what they owe, such as credit card debt, a mortgage, lines of credit, and so on. This knowledge will be essential if you’re granted power of attorney to take over your loved one’s finances. • Look for tax breaks available to caregivers. If you’re a caregiver, you may have to pay for some care costs out of pocket. Consequently, you could receive some tax credits and deductions. These benefits vary by state, so you’ll want to consult with your tax advisor to determine your eligibility. • Ensure necessary legal documents are in place. articles.text: Editor: Over the last five years, I’ve had the privilege of knowing Ruchi Medhekar and working together with her as co-room parents and during her time as VP and President of Beach Parents Organization. Based on those experiences, I enthusiastically endorse her for school board. Beyond Beach, Ruchi has been very active with district-wide initiatives and in the greater Piedmont community. Her experiences serving on PUSD’s TriSchool Site Council, the LCAP committee, Budget Advisory Committee as well as being on the board of the Piedmont Education Foundation have provided opportunities for her to learn about district operations, build consensus among different stakeholders, and develop a strong understanding of our community’s challenges and opportunities. Along with her peers in the Piedmont Recreation Commission, earlier this week she voted for the creation of a subcommittee to explore how Schoolmates can best serve the needs of families. However, the impact Ruchi has made in Piedmont extends well beyond her official resume. For example, because of her dedication to academic excellence and her desire to build an inspiring environment where students and teachers thrive, she has proactively elevated experts’ voices (for example in literacy) to explore how we can best serve our students in the district. Ruchi takes the time to educate herself, ask thoughtful questions, and truly listen before coming to a conclusion. Once informed, Ruchi’s passionate and collaborative approach puts people at ease
articles.title: Ruchi is invested in our collective success

I look forward to casting my vote for Jen Long for Piedmont City Council on November 8. –Amy McKenzie

All our conversations revolve around what school board members can do to maintain and enhance educational excellence,” he said. After announcing that a candidates’ forum would be held on September 22 in the high school library, all three candidates accepted an invitation on August 25 to attend. They were asked to answer questions either at the forum or in private beforehand. Candidates were notified that the forum would be recorded on video for posterity and accountability. “One candidate was uncomfortable with video recording, fearing it could create a gotcha situation in the future,” noted Titan. “Another candidate hired a campaign manager in early September who expressed discomfort with the PEEP forum in its entirety. On Friday, September 16, six days in advance, I received notice from campaign managers for Ruchi Medhekar and Lindsay Thomasson that those candidates had been advised to not attend the PEEP Forum. Titan spent the next several days trying to get clarity on their awareness of the broad advertisement of the forum to the entire city, including a front-page announcement in the September 14 issue of the Piedmont Post, and informal approval of all PEEP questions by School Superintendent Donald Evans. On September 20 candidate Shirley Hooi agreed to fill out the PEEP questions but canceled her attendance at the forum the next day. Titan then emailed everyone who had signed up for the forum to notify them that the three candidates had withdrawn and would not be attending. “Because it appears that two candidates were highly distrustful of the PEEP questions, our organization is making the questions available to readers of the Piedmont Post to let them make their own judgment,” said Titan. Multiple choice answers include options of what the current board behavior has been, what past candidates did, as well as some choices coming up. LET US VOTE BRIDGET HARRIS for CITY COUNCIL Donations can be sent to Bridget Harris Piedmont City Council at 6114 La Salle Avenue, #300, Oakland, CA 94611 PRIORITIES for PIEDMONT A friend recently said to me “the Housing Element was not an issue until it became an issue.” This is so true. I believe most Piedmont residents were not aware or focused on the Housing Element until the City Council presented a draft plan and that plan included downtown Piedmont, the Highland grassy strip, the Corey Reich Tennis Courts, and the Piedmont Center for the Arts. At that point the Housing Element became an issue for many; objections were raised. The latest plan pushes most of the units to Grand Avenue and Moraga Avenue. Grand Avenue is an appropriate location for multi-family units in that it is an area that is considered “walkable oriented development”. Park Boulevard is also an appropriate location. Both Grand and Park provide residents walkable options to grocery stores, hardware stores and other services as well as accessible transportation. The Piedmont Center for the Arts (801 Magnolia) and the Moraga Avenue locations, such as Blair Park, are not suitable locations for several reasons. 1 There has been little, or no analysis of the impact multi-family units will have on traffic, water, students, and safety. 2 Moraga Avenue is already very congested at certain times of the day; adding more cars will make it worse for both Oakland and Piedmont residents. 3 Both locations are in Zone B which is park and public lands. Multi-family units are only allowed in Zone C. Multifamily units are not allowed in Zone B. The Proposed change to the zones requires a vote. Section 9.02 of Piedmont’s City Charter states "The Council may classify and reclassify the zones established, but …no existing zones shall be reclassified without submitting the question to a vote at a general or special election." The city’s zoning ordinance, codified in Section 17.02.010 of Piedmont’s Municipal Code states “…the prohibition not to reduce, enlarge, or reclassify a zone without a vote is understood to mean the city may not change zone boundaries, or change (reclassify) a property from one zone to another.” Piedmont has Five Zones: A- Single Family Residential B- Public land C- Multi-family Residential D- Commercial and Mixed Use, and E- Estate Residential. Presently Zone B does not allow for Multi-family Residential, which is only allowed in Zone C. Likewise Zone B does not allow for Mixed-use commercial/residential development which is currently only allowed in Zone D. The current City Council position is that NO vote is required for the Council to allow Multi-family Residential and Mixed-Use/Commercial in Zone B. Recently the City defended its position that a vote is not needed. The City stated that “The adoption of a Draft Housing Element does not enact any modifications to the Zoning Ordinance. The Draft Housing Element includes policies and programs that call for revisions to the Zoning Ordinance that allow for ….” multi-family units. More…flip side www.bridgetforpiedmont.com

BRIDGET HARRIS for CITY COUNCIL PRIORITIES for PIEDMONT The City goes on to say that after the Housing Element is approved by the state, then the City will implement modifications to the Zoning Ordinance. There is no provision for a vote; instead, the City takes us through four administrative steps to validate the proposed changes to Zone B. 1. 2. 3. 4. The City states that revisions to the Zoning Ordinance require “several public meetings”. The revisions will be posted for public comment. The Planning Commission will make final recommendations to the City Council. The City Council twice reads the revisions to the City Code , then the revisions become law. (See https://www.piedmontishome.org/faqs) If that were true, there is no reason the City Council could not make the same changes to Zone A which is single family residences. The City plans to push forward its agenda to rezone areas, even though our charter and our municipal code clearly state that any changes, any reclassifications, and any enlargements require approval by Piedmont voters. The City further states “The Charter does not require a vote if the City changes uses or density within a zone.” Changing the density of 801 Magnolia and Blair Park to allow 100+ multi-family units is a re-zone no matter what language is used. Revising the City Code as proposed is just a euphemism for re-zoning and violates both the spirit and the letter of the City Charter. If I am elected, I will strive to make sure any re-zone, revision, change in classification, or increase in density in Piedmont is brought to a vote of all the voters in Piedmont, not just the City Council. Safety and Infrastructure. The Piedmont community greatly values its police and fire departments, yet both operate in outdated and unsafe facilities. In 2020 the City Council discussed deficiencies in the buildings and noncompliance with the state’s Essential Services Act. At that time the Council considered improving the facilities with funding by issuance of public safety bonds. For various reasons, including the pandemic and the focus on the pool, the project did not move forward. Modernizing Piedmont’s public infrastructure is vital to our future. Our community came together for the Aquatic Center, approving a bond measure, and we can repeat that success to rebuild our City Hall and public safety buildings. I will clearly explain the issues and the need for renovations and then provide detailed options and costs before asking for increases in fees, taxes, or approval of any bond measure. I am a tax attorney, working with clients in many different industries. I have been involved for many years on various finance committees. The community deserves excellent public safety services, and we must insure those services by capital investment in City Hall and the police and fire department infrastructure. I am certain our City can find the ways and means to complete the renovations needed to improve Piedmont's infrastructure – but we need community involvement in this process. We need to vote. www.bridgetforpiedmont.com Donations can be sent to Bridget Harris Piedmont City Council at 6114 La Salle Avenue, #300, Oakland, CA 94611
